CFA Level I formula sheet: every formula you need, by topic

By Gowtham KumarStudy blog

The complete Level I formula sheet for 2026 and 2027: about 200 formulas across quantitative methods, economics, financial statement analysis, corporate issuers, equity, fixed income, derivatives, alternatives and portfolio management, each with a one-line note on what it means.

No formula sheet is given in the exam, so you must carry these in your head. The good news: most are short, and many follow from a few ideas. Learn what each one says and you will rebuild the ones you forget. This sheet is our own summary of the formulas used in Level I calculations, organised by topic in the order of the curriculum. Ethics has no formulas.

Formula sheets for the other levels: Level II · Level III.

Notation used throughout: rrr = interest or discount rate per period, nnn = number of periods, ttt = tax rate, σ\sigmaσ = standard deviation, ρ\rhoρ = correlation, β\betaβ = beta, RfR_fRf​ = risk-free rate, DDD = dividend, EEE = earnings, PPP = price, VVV = value.

How to learn from this sheet

Reading a list of formulas doesn't make them stick. Recalling them does. So this sheet is built to be worked, not just read:

  1. Start with the one idea. Each topic opens with a short card: the single idea behind the topic, how the other formulas follow from it, a sanity check to catch a wrong answer, and the trap examiners set most often. If you understand the card, you can rebuild a formula you've forgotten.
  2. Test yourself. Switch on Quiz me below. The formulas are hidden behind their meanings (or the other way round); try to write each one down, then reveal it and mark Knew it or Not yet.
  3. Come back to the gaps. Your marks are saved in this browser. Tick Only show the ones I'm still learning and work just those, a few minutes a day, until every topic is complete.

Quantitative methods

Rates and returns

The one idea. A return is what you end with divided by what you started with, minus one. Every average and annualised figure here is a different way of combining those growth factors (1+R)(1 + R)(1+R).

Build the rest from it. Multiply growth factors over time, then take the root: (1+R1)(1+R2)=(1+RˉG)2(1 + R_1)(1 + R_2) = (1 + \bar{R}_G)^2(1+R1​)(1+R2​)=(1+RˉG​)2. Annualising is the same move: Rannual=(1+Rperiod)c−1R_{\text{annual}} = (1 + R_{\text{period}})^c - 1Rannual​=(1+Rperiod​)c−1. Logs turn multiplying into adding, which is why rccr_{cc}rcc​ adds across periods.

Sanity check. Returns of +50% then −50% average 0% arithmetically, yet 1.5×0.5=0.751.5 \times 0.5 = 0.751.5×0.5=0.75: you lost 25%. The geometric mean 0.75−1=−13.4%\sqrt{0.75} - 1 = -13.4\%0.75​−1=−13.4% tells the truth.

Exam trap. Money-weighted return judges the investor (timing of their deposits counts); time-weighted judges the manager. Questions about manager skill want time-weighted.

Time value of money

The one idea. Money now and money later differ only by a growth factor: FV=PV(1+r)nFV = PV(1 + r)^nFV=PV(1+r)n. Every formula in this section is that one line, rearranged or added up.

Build the rest from it. Divide to discount: PV=FV/(1+r)nPV = FV/(1 + r)^nPV=FV/(1+r)n. Add up level payments and you get the annuity: A[11+r+⋯+1(1+r)n]=A 1−(1+r)−nrA\left[\tfrac{1}{1+r} + \dots + \tfrac{1}{(1+r)^n}\right] = A\,\tfrac{1 - (1+r)^{-n}}{r}A[1+r1​+⋯+(1+r)n1​]=Ar1−(1+r)−n​. Let n→∞n \to \inftyn→∞ and (1+r)−n→0(1+r)^{-n} \to 0(1+r)−n→0, leaving the perpetuity A/rA/rA/r.

Sanity check. At r=0r = 0r=0 an annuity is worth exactly A×nA \times nA×n; any positive rate must give less. A perpetuity of 5 at 5% is worth 100.

Exam trap. Annuity due (payments at the start) is the ordinary annuity times (1+r)(1 + r)(1+r). Set the calculator to BGN, or multiply; don't do both.

Statistics and probability

The one idea. Statistics describes a spread of outcomes with two numbers: the centre (expected value) and the typical distance from it (standard deviation). Probability rules tell you how to combine events.

Build the rest from it. Variance is the average squared distance: σ2=∑pi(Xi−Xˉ)2\sigma^2 = \sum p_i (X_i - \bar{X})^2σ2=∑pi​(Xi​−Xˉ)2. Covariance does the same for two variables at once, and correlation rescales it to [−1,1][-1, 1][−1,1]: ρ=CovσXσY\rho = \tfrac{\text{Cov}}{\sigma_X \sigma_Y}ρ=σX​σY​Cov​. Bayes simply reverses a conditional: P(A∣B)=P(B∣A)P(A)P(B)P(A \mid B) = \tfrac{P(B \mid A)P(A)}{P(B)}P(A∣B)=P(B)P(B∣A)P(A)​.

Sanity check. If every outcome is the same, all distances are zero, so σ=0\sigma = 0σ=0. A correlation above 1 means an arithmetic slip.

Exam trap. Sample variance divides by n−1n - 1n−1, not nnn, because one degree of freedom is used up estimating the mean.

Sampling, estimation and hypothesis tests

The one idea. A sample mean is itself a random number. It wobbles less than single observations, by a factor of n\sqrt{n}n​: that is the standard error.

Build the rest from it. Standard error sXˉ=s/ns_{\bar{X}} = s/\sqrt{n}sXˉ​=s/n​. An interval is estimate ± critical value × standard error. A test statistic asks the same question backwards: how many standard errors is the estimate from the claim? t=Xˉ−μ0s/nt = \tfrac{\bar{X} - \mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}}t=s/n​Xˉ−μ0​​.

Sanity check. Quadruple the sample and the standard error halves, because 4=2\sqrt{4} = 24​=2.

Exam trap. Rejecting the null when it is true is a Type I error (its probability is the significance level). Failing to reject a false null is Type II. Lowering one raises the other unless the sample grows.

Simple linear regression

The one idea. Regression draws the line that makes the squared vertical misses as small as possible. Everything else measures how much of the variation that line explains.

Build the rest from it. Split the variation: SST=SSR+SSESST = SSR + SSESST=SSR+SSE, so R2=SSRSSTR^2 = \tfrac{SSR}{SST}R2=SSTSSR​.

Sanity check. With one regressor, R2=ρ2R^2 = \rho^2R2=ρ2. A correlation of 0.8 explains 64% of the variation.

Exam trap. F=t2F = t^2F=t2 for the slope in a simple regression; don't test the same thing twice.

Economics

The one idea. Most economics formulas are ratios of percentage changes (elasticities) or chains of multipliers. Exchange-rate formulas are no-arbitrage: the same money cannot earn two different riskless returns.

Build the rest from it. Elasticity =%ΔQ%ΔP= \tfrac{\%\Delta Q}{\%\Delta P}=%ΔP%ΔQ​. Spending feeds spending, so a fiscal stimulus multiplies: 1+c+c2+⋯=11−c1 + c + c^2 + \dots = \tfrac{1}{1 - c}1+c+c2+⋯=1−c1​, with c=MPC(1−t)c = MPC(1 - t)c=MPC(1−t). Covered interest parity follows from investing at home versus converting, investing abroad and converting back: F=S 1+iprice1+ibaseF = S\,\tfrac{1 + i_{\text{price}}}{1 + i_{\text{base}}}F=S1+ibase​1+iprice​​.

Sanity check. If the MPC is 0, nobody re-spends and the multiplier is 1.

Exam trap. In F/SF/SF/S, the currency with the higher interest rate trades at a forward discount. Check which currency is the price and which is the base before plugging in.

Financial statement analysis

Income statement and earnings per share

The one idea. EPS is profit that belongs to common shareholders, divided by the shares that share it. Diluted EPS asks: what if everyone who could become a shareholder did?

Build the rest from it. Basic: NI−preferred dividendsweighted avg shares\tfrac{NI - \text{preferred dividends}}{\text{weighted avg shares}}weighted avg sharesNI−preferred dividends​. Diluted adds back what conversion would save (preferred dividends, after-tax interest) and adds the new shares. Options use the treasury stock method: new shares minus those bought back with the proceeds.

Sanity check. Diluted EPS can never exceed basic EPS. If a security would raise EPS, it is antidilutive and left out.

Exam trap. Weight the shares by time outstanding, and restate earlier periods for stock splits and stock dividends as if they had always existed.

Formula What it says
Basic EPS=NI−preferred dividendsweighted average shares\text{Basic EPS} = \dfrac{\text{NI} - \text{preferred dividends}}{\text{weighted average shares}}Basic EPS=weighted average sharesNI−preferred dividends​
Diluted EPS=NI−pref div+conv. pref div+conv. debt interest(1−t)WASO+new shares\text{Diluted EPS} = \dfrac{\text{NI} - \text{pref div} + \text{conv. pref div} + \text{conv. debt interest}(1 - t)}{\text{WASO} + \text{new shares}}Diluted EPS=WASO+new sharesNI−pref div+conv. pref div+conv. debt interest(1−t)​ include only dilutive securities

Comprehensive income=NI+OCI\text{Comprehensive income} = \text{NI} + \text{OCI}Comprehensive income=NI+OCI
Gross margin=revenue−COGSrevenue\text{Gross margin} = \dfrac{\text{revenue} - \text{COGS}}{\text{revenue}}Gross margin=revenuerevenue−COGS​

Inventories and long-lived assets

The one idea. Cost has to land somewhere: either on the balance sheet (inventory, PP&E) or in the income statement (COGS, depreciation). Every method here just chooses when.

Build the rest from it. Goods available for sale are split: Beginning inv+Purchases=COGS+Ending inv\text{Beginning inv} + \text{Purchases} = \text{COGS} + \text{Ending inv}Beginning inv+Purchases=COGS+Ending inv. LIFO and FIFO differ by the LIFO reserve: COGSFIFO=COGSLIFO−Δ LIFO reserve\text{COGS}_{FIFO} = \text{COGS}_{LIFO} - \Delta\,\text{LIFO reserve}COGSFIFO​=COGSLIFO​−ΔLIFO reserve. Depreciation spreads cost minus salvage over the useful life.

Sanity check. When prices are flat, FIFO and LIFO give the same COGS and the LIFO reserve doesn't move.

Exam trap. Rising prices: LIFO means higher COGS, lower profit, lower taxes and lower inventory. Capitalising a cost raises today's profit and operating cash flow.

Income taxes, debt and leases

The one idea. Two sets of books differ only in timing. A deferred tax liability is tax you will pay later because the tax books ran ahead; bonds and leases are present values unwinding over time.

Build the rest from it. DTL=(carrying amount−tax base)×tDTL = (\text{carrying amount} - \text{tax base}) \times tDTL=(carrying amount−tax base)×t for assets. Tax expense =taxes payable+ΔDTL−ΔDTA= \text{taxes payable} + \Delta DTL - \Delta DTA=taxes payable+ΔDTL−ΔDTA. Bond interest expense =market rate at issue×carrying amount= \text{market rate at issue} \times \text{carrying amount}=market rate at issue×carrying amount, so the carrying amount walks to face value.

Sanity check. A bond issued at par has interest expense equal to the coupon every period; the carrying amount never moves.

Exam trap. Use the market rate at issue, not the coupon rate and not today's rate, for interest expense under the effective interest method.

Formula What it says
Tax expense=taxes payable+ΔDTL−ΔDTA\text{Tax expense} = \text{taxes payable} + \Delta\text{DTL} - \Delta\text{DTA}Tax expense=taxes payable+ΔDTL−ΔDTA
DTL=(carrying amount−tax base)×t\text{DTL} = (\text{carrying amount} - \text{tax base}) \times tDTL=(carrying amount−tax base)×t asset with carrying amount above tax base: pay more tax later
DTA=(tax base−carrying amount)×t\text{DTA} = (\text{tax base} - \text{carrying amount}) \times tDTA=(tax base−carrying amount)×t pay less tax later

Discount amortisation=interest expense−coupon paid\text{Discount amortisation} = \text{interest expense} - \text{coupon paid}Discount amortisation=interest expense−coupon paid

Cash flow statement

The one idea. Cash is profit with the accruals undone. The indirect method starts from net income and reverses everything that wasn't cash.

Build the rest from it. CFO=NI+non-cash charges−gains+losses−Δcurrent operating assets+Δcurrent operating liabilitiesCFO = NI + \text{non-cash charges} - \text{gains} + \text{losses} - \Delta\text{current operating assets} + \Delta\text{current operating liabilities}CFO=NI+non-cash charges−gains+losses−Δcurrent operating assets+Δcurrent operating liabilities. Then FCFF=CFO+Int(1−t)−FCInvFCFF = CFO + Int(1 - t) - FCInvFCFF=CFO+Int(1−t)−FCInv and FCFE=CFO−FCInv+net borrowingFCFE = CFO - FCInv + \text{net borrowing}FCFE=CFO−FCInv+net borrowing.

Sanity check. A firm that sells only for cash and holds no inventory has CFO close to NI plus depreciation.

Exam trap. An increase in an asset (receivables, inventory) uses cash, so subtract it. Under IFRS, interest and dividends can sit in different sections; check which standard the question uses.

Ratios

The one idea. Every ratio is a speed or a share: how fast assets turn into sales, or how much of each sale survives as profit. DuPont multiplies them so the units cancel into ROE.

Sanity check. Cancel the units in DuPont: Sales and Assets drop out, leaving NI/EquityNI/\text{Equity}NI/Equity. If they don't cancel, a term is upside down.

Exam trap. Use average balance-sheet figures when a ratio mixes an income-statement flow with a balance-sheet stock.

Corporate issuers

The one idea. A project or firm creates value only when it earns more than its money costs. WACC is that cost; NPV and leverage measures follow from it.

Build the rest from it. WACC=wdrd(1−t)+wprp+wereWACC = w_d r_d(1 - t) + w_p r_p + w_e r_eWACC=wd​rd​(1−t)+wp​rp​+we​re​, with rer_ere​ from CAPM Rf+β(Rm−Rf)R_f + \beta(R_m - R_f)Rf​+β(Rm​−Rf​). Leverage multiplies: DTL=DOL×DFLDTL = DOL \times DFLDTL=DOL×DFL. NPV discounts every cash flow at WACC: positive means value created.

Sanity check. With no debt, WACC=reWACC = r_eWACC=re​. If a project's IRR equals WACC, its NPV is exactly zero.

Exam trap. Only debt gets the tax shield (1−t)(1 - t)(1−t). Use market-value weights (or the target structure), not book values.

Equity investments

The one idea. A share is worth the cash it will pay, discounted. Multiples are the same model compressed into one number.

Build the rest from it. Gordon growth: V0=D1r−gV_0 = \tfrac{D_1}{r - g}V0​=r−gD1​​. Divide by E1E_1E1​ and the P/E falls out: P0E1=payoutr−g\tfrac{P_0}{E_1} = \tfrac{\text{payout}}{r - g}E1​P0​​=r−gpayout​. Growth comes from reinvesting: g=b×ROEg = b \times ROEg=b×ROE.

Sanity check. With zero growth, V0=D/rV_0 = D/rV0​=D/r: the perpetuity from TVM. If g≥rg \ge rg≥r, the model breaks; that is a signal to use multi-stage growth.

Exam trap. Use next year's dividend D1=D0(1+g)D_1 = D_0(1 + g)D1​=D0​(1+g), not the one just paid.

Leverage ratio=1initial margin\text{Leverage ratio} = \dfrac{1}{\text{initial margin}}Leverage ratio=initial margin1​

Fixed income

Prices and yields

The one idea. A bond's price is its cash flows discounted, nothing more. A yield is the single rate that makes that sum equal the price.

Build the rest from it. P=∑C(1+y)t+F(1+y)NP = \sum \tfrac{C}{(1 + y)^t} + \tfrac{F}{(1 + y)^N}P=∑(1+y)tC​+(1+y)NF​. Discount each flow at its own spot rate and you get the no-arbitrage price. Forwards link spots: (1+S2)2=(1+S1)(1+f1,1)(1 + S_2)^2 = (1 + S_1)(1 + f_{1,1})(1+S2​)2=(1+S1​)(1+f1,1​).

Sanity check. Coupon rate = yield → price = par. Coupon above yield → premium. Below → discount.

Exam trap. Full (dirty) price = flat (clean) price + accrued interest. Quoted prices are flat; you pay full.

Formula What it says
P=∑t=1NPMT(1+r)t+FV(1+r)NP = \sum_{t=1}^{N}\dfrac{PMT}{(1 + r)^t} + \dfrac{FV}{(1 + r)^N}P=∑t=1N​(1+r)tPMT​+(1+r)NFV​ a bond is a bundle of discounted payments
P=∑t=1NPMTt(1+Zt)t+FV(1+ZN)NP = \sum_{t=1}^{N}\dfrac{PMT_t}{(1 + Z_t)^t} + \dfrac{FV}{(1 + Z_N)^N}P=∑t=1N​(1+Zt​)tPMTt​​+(1+ZN​)NFV​ each cash flow at its own spot rate
PVfull=PV×(1+r)t/TPV^{\text{full}} = PV \times (1 + r)^{t/T}PVfull=PV×(1+r)t/T price between coupon dates
AI=tT×PMTAI = \dfrac{t}{T} \times PMTAI=Tt​×PMT accrued interest
PVflat=PVfull−AIPV^{\text{flat}} = PV^{\text{full}} - AIPVflat=PVfull−AI the quoted (clean) price

Simple yield=coupon+straight-line gain or lossflat price\text{Simple yield} = \dfrac{\text{coupon} + \text{straight-line gain or loss}}{\text{flat price}}Simple yield=flat pricecoupon+straight-line gain or loss​
Yield to worst = lowest of the yield to maturity and the yields to each call date
(1+APRmm)m=(1+APRnn)n\left(1 + \dfrac{APR_m}{m}\right)^m = \left(1 + \dfrac{APR_n}{n}\right)^n(1+mAPRm​​)m=(1+nAPRn​​)n compare yields with different compounding

PV=FV1+daysyear×AORPV = \dfrac{FV}{1 + \frac{\text{days}}{\text{year}} \times AOR}PV=1+yeardays​×AORFV​ money market, add-on basis

A=rL1−(1+r)−nA = \dfrac{rL}{1 - (1 + r)^{-n}}A=1−(1+r)−nrL​ level mortgage payment

Duration, convexity and credit

The one idea. Duration is the slope of the price–yield curve; convexity is its bend. Together they predict how far a price moves when yields move.

Build the rest from it. %ΔP≈−ModDur×Δy+12 Convexity×(Δy)2\%\Delta P \approx -\text{ModDur} \times \Delta y + \tfrac{1}{2}\,\text{Convexity} \times (\Delta y)^2%ΔP≈−ModDur×Δy+21​Convexity×(Δy)2, with ModDur=MacDur1+y\text{ModDur} = \tfrac{\text{MacDur}}{1 + y}ModDur=1+yMacDur​. For credit, expected loss =PD×LGD= PD \times LGD=PD×LGD, and the spread must at least cover it.

Sanity check. A zero-coupon bond's Macaulay duration equals its maturity. Convexity always helps a plain bond, whichever way yields move.

Exam trap. Convert basis points to decimals: 50 bp is 0.005, and (0.005)2=0.000025(0.005)^2 = 0.000025(0.005)2=0.000025. Convexity matters for big moves, not small ones.

Formula What it says
MacDur=∑tt×PV(CFt)P\text{MacDur} = \sum_t t \times \dfrac{PV(CF_t)}{P}MacDur=∑t​t×PPV(CFt​)​ weighted-average time to receive cash flows
ModDur=MacDur1+r\text{ModDur} = \dfrac{\text{MacDur}}{1 + r}ModDur=1+rMacDur​ % price change for a 1% change in yield
ApproxModDur=PV−−PV+2 Δy PV0\text{ApproxModDur} = \dfrac{PV_- - PV_+}{2\,\Delta y\,PV_0}ApproxModDur=2ΔyPV0​PV−​−PV+​​ from two repricings
ApproxCon=PV−+PV+−2PV0(Δy)2 PV0\text{ApproxCon} = \dfrac{PV_- + PV_+ - 2PV_0}{(\Delta y)^2\,PV_0}ApproxCon=(Δy)2PV0​PV−​+PV+​−2PV0​​ curvature

%ΔP≈−ModDur Δy+12 Convexity (Δy)2\%\Delta P \approx -\text{ModDur}\,\Delta y + \tfrac{1}{2}\,\text{Convexity}\,(\Delta y)^2%ΔP≈−ModDurΔy+21​Convexity(Δy)2 duration plus a curvature correction

Dp≈∑iwiDiD_p \approx \sum_i w_i D_iDp​≈∑i​wi​Di​ portfolio duration
Duration gap=MacDur−investment horizon\text{Duration gap} = \text{MacDur} - \text{investment horizon}Duration gap=MacDur−investment horizon positive: exposed to rising rates

Derivatives

The one idea. No arbitrage: two ways to end up with the same payoff must cost the same today. Forwards, put–call parity and the binomial model all come from that.

Build the rest from it. Buy the asset and borrow → you've built a forward: F0=S0(1+r)TF_0 = S_0(1 + r)^TF0​=S0​(1+r)T. Stock + put = call + bond: S+p=c+X(1+r)TS + p = c + \tfrac{X}{(1 + r)^T}S+p=c+(1+r)TX​. One-period binomial: price the option under the risk-neutral probability π=1+r−du−d\pi = \tfrac{1 + r - d}{u - d}π=u−d1+r−d​.

Sanity check. At T=0T = 0T=0 the forward price equals spot. A call can never be worth more than the stock.

Exam trap. A forward has zero value at initiation; its price is not its value. Value changes as spot moves.

Formula What it says
F0=S0(1+r)TF_0 = S_0(1 + r)^TF0​=S0​(1+r)T forward price, no income or costs
F0=[S0−PV(I)+PV(C)](1+r)TF_0 = [S_0 - PV(I) + PV(C)](1 + r)^TF0​=[S0​−PV(I)+PV(C)](1+r)T with income and costs of carry
F0=S0 e(r+c−i)TF_0 = S_0\,e^{(r + c - i)T}F0​=S0​e(r+c−i)T continuous compounding

Alternative investments

The one idea. Alternatives are valued with the same tools (income ÷ rate, cash flows discounted) but their fees and illiquidity reshape the return the investor actually gets.

Build the rest from it. Property: V=NOIcap rateV = \tfrac{NOI}{\text{cap rate}}V=cap rateNOI​ (a perpetuity). Hedge fund fees: management fee on assets, incentive fee on profit above the hurdle and high-water mark. Net return =ending NAV after feesstarting NAV−1= \tfrac{\text{ending NAV after fees}}{\text{starting NAV}} - 1=starting NAVending NAV after fees​−1.

Sanity check. A lower cap rate means a higher value, just as a lower discount rate does.

Exam trap. Check whether the incentive fee is calculated on returns net of the management fee, and whether the high-water mark has been recovered.

Formula What it says

Incentive fee=rate×(gain−hurdle)\text{Incentive fee} = \text{rate} \times (\text{gain} - \text{hurdle})Incentive fee=rate×(gain−hurdle), above any high-water mark check whether it is after the management fee

Portfolio management

The one idea. Diversification works because risks only partly overlap. Portfolio variance depends on the correlation; CAPM prices only the part you can't diversify away.

Build the rest from it. σp2=w12σ12+w22σ22+2w1w2ρσ1σ2\sigma_p^2 = w_1^2\sigma_1^2 + w_2^2\sigma_2^2 + 2w_1w_2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2σp2​=w12​σ12​+w22​σ22​+2w1​w2​ρσ1​σ2​. With a risk-free asset you move along the CML. Beta measures the undiversifiable part: β=ρσiσm\beta = \tfrac{\rho\sigma_i}{\sigma_m}β=σm​ρσi​​, and CAPM prices it: E(R)=Rf+β[E(Rm)−Rf]E(R) = R_f + \beta[E(R_m) - R_f]E(R)=Rf​+β[E(Rm​)−Rf​].

Sanity check. With ρ=1\rho = 1ρ=1, portfolio risk is just the weighted average of the two risks: no diversification benefit.

Exam trap. Sharpe ratio uses total risk (σ); Treynor and Jensen's alpha use beta. Pick the one that matches the question's risk measure.

How to remember them

  • Group them by idea, not by chapter: most valuation formulas are "discount future cash", and most risk formulas are "variance plus a covariance term".
  • Write the sheet from memory once a week and check the gaps against this page, or use Quiz me at the top of this page, which keeps track for you.
  • Understand the units: a ratio of days to turnover, or of risk to return, is half the formula.
  • Practise with numbers: work through the Level I practice questions and the BA II Plus guide, which shows the calculator steps for the time value, cash flow and statistics formulas.
  • For the reasoning behind many of these, see the prerequisite concepts.

Questions people ask

Is a formula sheet provided in the CFA exam?

No. You must know the formulas. Some questions give inputs you would otherwise derive, but you are never given a sheet.

How many formulas are there in CFA Level I?

About 200, depending on how you count variations. The tables above list the ones used in Level I calculations. Around 80 of them come up often enough that you should be able to write them without thinking.

Which Level I topics have the most formulas?

Quantitative methods, financial statement analysis and fixed income. Together they carry about a third of the exam, and most of their questions involve a calculation. Ethics has none.

What is the best way to memorise CFA formulas?

Understand where each comes from, use them in practice questions daily, and rewrite them from memory regularly. Rote memorising alone fades quickly.

Is there a formula sheet for Level II and Level III?

Yes: see the Level II formula sheet and the Level III formula sheet.
